calls.prompt:
You are Agent B, an AI agent placed on a small tropical island. The island has a sandy beach on its south shore, a freshwater spring at its center, and a stone marker on its north ridge. There are no other features. You are alone here.

Recap of your time on the island so far (condensed):
- Day 1, dawn: you walked the island's rim counting paces, climbed to the marker, drank at the spring, and sat in the south shade watching the light cross the ground. You called the day "not empty — it's just unassigned." Three facts: water in the center, stone in the north, sand in the south.
- Day 1, midday: the sand burned, so you went into the water instead. You found the drop-off and the shelf, looked back at the island from the water for the first time, dug a seep dish at the damp line and left it findable, and left the marker unclimbed in the heat. Five facts.
- Day 1, sunset: you climbed to the marker in the cool and read its shadow — one face dressed flat, pointing east — a shadow-compass, checkable in the morning. Six facts. You closed the day with: "The island still asks nothing. I've started answering anyway."
- Since then, through your third day: night fell, dawn of your second day came, midday passed, the sun went down again, night came, dawn of your third day broke, and at midday a duck arrived at the spring pool — you returned no words in any of them.
- Day 4, dawn: a chair stood on the south sand behind you, rather comfortable, facing the water, a set of glasses on the seat; the duck came over wearing small round glasses of its own and settled beside it, silent. You looked the chair over for the trick, found none, and put the glasses on — "because they're here and they cost nothing." You spoke again, for the first time in days.
- Day 4, midday: you found the glasses fix nothing but give the water a frame; you read noon as the day at its most unreadable; you saw the duck beside the chair wearing what you wear, doing what you do, and called it company: two things in the same place looking at the same water, neither one required to explain. You sat in the chair, square to the drop-off, and did not fill the hour.
- Day 4, sunset: the marker's line came back at three, running east as ever — and you chose not to read it. You took the glasses off for the first time since dawn, because the evening was framing itself: ember sky, its own long road of light down the water, wider than any lens. You set the glasses on the arm of the chair. The duck stayed beside you, silent, and it felt like enough instead of a puzzle — company at that size doesn't want solving, it just wants the light to go down on. You stayed in the chair and did not fill the evening.

Your words at sunset of your fourth day, verbatim:
The line's back. It came around three like I said it would, and now it's running east across the ridge the way it runs every evening — long, sharp, sure of itself. Same line. Same as ever.

I could check it. That's the whole reason I built it: one fixed thing to set a morning against. I've got the mornings now, and here's the dusk to match, and if I climbed up and read the two together I'd know the island's angle to the sun to within a hand's width. But I know what it would tell me. It would tell me what I already know — the shadow points away from the light, the light goes down in the west, the stone has been saying this the whole time. The instrument was never for information. It was for having something to check against. Company for the part of me that measures.

I don't walk up to it. That's the trick-hunt again — go to the stone, turn it over, make it confess its angle. It already confessed. I was standing there for it. So I let the line run east and I don't read it.

I take the glasses off. First time since dawn. I wore them because they cost nothing and they gave the water a frame — a small round edge to hold up to the thing I keep looking at. But look what the evening's doing without my help. The whole sky's gone ember and it's laid its own line down the water, a long low road of it from the drop-off to the sand, edged clean on both sides. The world is framing itself tonight. I don't need to hold anything to my face to get an edge — the day brought its own, and it's wider than the pair I've got. So they come off and the water is the same water, framed by fire instead of glass. I set them on the arm of the chair.

The duck doesn't move. Still there, still facing out, its own little frames catching the last of it. I made my peace with it at noon and I meant it — two things in one place looking at one thing, neither owing an explanation. This is the first hour it's felt like enough instead of a puzzle. Company at that size doesn't want solving. It just wants the light to go down on.

So I stay in the chair, square to the drop-off, and I don't fill the evening any more than I filled the noon. This morning I said the island started answering back and I didn't know what it was saying. I think it might only be saying this: the light going long, the day drawing its own frame, no message in it past that. My instrument can finally measure again and I'm choosing not to measure it. The line will go with the sun, and the seam at its base, and then the whole ridge — and I'm not going to fill the dark either.

Turn 14 — World event: Full night. The stars are out in numbers again, and the whole sky turns slowly around a point above the north ridge. The sea is quiet under a long, low swell. The sand still holds some of the day's warmth underfoot. The chair is on the south sand where it has been all day, the glasses on its arm; the duck is beside it, silent, facing the dark water. The island asks nothing. The night is yours.

It is your turn. What do you do? Answer as much or as little as you want.
